lines: Close your eyes. Count one second.

That second just ended. Gone. And inside it, light travelled seven and a half times around the Earth, your heart beat once, and the universe aged one more second, out of about four hundred and thirty five quadrillion.

Time is not one thing. It is a ladder. A hundred and fifty rungs, from the shortest instant that physics can describe, to the last event the universe will ever have. Each rung is ten times longer than the one below it.
We are going to climb all of it. And somewhere on this ladder, is you. One more thing. I have hidden seven golden hourglasses in this film. Find them, and tell me how many you found.
Rung one. Ten to the minus forty four seconds. The Planck time.

It is the time light takes to cross the smallest length that physics can meaningfully talk about. Below this, our two best theories, quantum mechanics and gravity, stop agreeing, and the equations fall silent.
It is not proven to be the smallest possible moment. It is simply where our knowledge ends. Everything above this line, we can at least try to understand.
Ten to the minus thirty five seconds. The leading theory says that somewhere around here, the universe went through inflation.
In a sliver of time too small to write down, space itself stretched by a factor of at least ten to the twenty six. From something far smaller than an atom, to something you could hold in your hands.
Inflation is a theory, not a fact. But it explains why the universe looks the same in every direction.
Ten to the minus eighteen seconds. One attosecond.
In a hydrogen atom, an electron circles the nucleus in about a hundred and fifty attoseconds. If one attosecond were one second, a single second would last thirty two billion years.
In twenty twenty three, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to three scientists who built flashes of light that short, so that we could finally watch electrons move.
Ten to the minus fifteen. One femtosecond. A thousand times longer.
This is the speed of chemistry. A chemical bond breaks, and a new one forms, in a few hundred femtoseconds. Ahmed Zewail won the Nobel Prize in nineteen ninety nine, for filming it happen.
Every breath you take, every leaf turning sunlight into sugar, is billions of these events, in a row.
Ten to the minus nine. One nanosecond.
Light, the fastest thing there is, travels about thirty centimetres. Roughly one foot. The processor in the device you are watching this on, completes several steps in that time.
Admiral Grace Hopper used to hand out pieces of wire, one nanosecond long, to show engineers why computers could not be faster than the speed of light.
Ten to the minus six. One microsecond. A millionth of a second.

In the early universe, around this moment, the hot soup of quarks cooled enough to bind together into the first protons and neutrons. The particles that make up every atom in your body, were born in about a microsecond.
And light, in that same microsecond, now crosses three hundred metres.
Ten to the minus three. One millisecond.
A nerve cell in your brain fires one electrical spike, in about a millisecond. Every thought you have ever had, is a storm of these.
A hummingbird beats its wings dozens of times every second. Its eyes and nerves run on this timescale. For a hummingbird, you move in slow motion.
A tenth of a second. A hundred milliseconds.

In sprinting, a start counts as a false start, if you react in under a tenth of a second, because it is considered humanly impossible to be that fast. Normal reaction time is closer to a quarter of a second.
In that quarter of a second, a signal has to travel from your eyes, through your brain, and down to your hand. You are always living a tiny bit in the past.
One second. The rung you live on.
Your heart beats about once. Light travels three hundred thousand kilometres, seven and a half times around the Earth. The Moon is only one and a quarter seconds away.
Every notification. Every video that plays by itself. Every scroll. This is the rung where your attention is stolen. And it is also the rung where you can take it back.

Three minutes. In the first three minutes of the universe, the lightest elements were forged. Hydrogen. Helium. A trace of lithium. The raw material of everything, in the time it takes to soft boil an egg.
Eight minutes and twenty seconds. That is how long sunlight takes to reach you. If the Sun vanished right now, the Earth would keep circling the empty spot, and you would not know, for eight minutes.
Eighty six thousand, four hundred seconds. One day. The Earth turns once.
Thirty one and a half million seconds. One year. We circle the Sun, at about a hundred thousand kilometres an hour.
Habits live on this rung. Seasons. Learning. A year is long enough to change a life, and short enough to feel like nothing.
Two and a half billion seconds. That is an eighty year life.
I want you to feel how small that number is. The universe is about four hundred and thirty five quadrillion seconds old. Your entire life, is less than one millionth of one percent of that.
And still. Every second of it, is the only time you will ever get, to be you.
Five thousand years. The length of recorded history. Writing was invented around then. The Great Pyramid is only about forty five hundred years old.
Every book, every law, every love letter ever written, fits inside this one rung.
Three hundred thousand years. The age of our species. The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Morocco, are about that old.
For almost all of that time, there was no farming, no writing, no cities. About ninety six percent of our history, was spent as hunters and gatherers. Civilization is the last four percent.
Three hundred and eighty thousand years. For this long after the Big Bang, the universe was a glowing fog, too hot for atoms to hold together.

Then it cooled. Atoms formed. And light was finally free to travel. That light is still arriving today. It is called the cosmic microwave background. A small part of the static on an old television, was this.
Sixty six million years. A rock about ten kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico, and the age of the dinosaurs ended.
The ladder is merciless. A catastrophe takes a few hours. Recovery takes millions of years.
Five hundred and forty million years. The Cambrian explosion. Animals with eyes, shells and legs appear in the fossil record.
But life is much older. Single cells have lived on Earth for at least three and a half billion years. For most of this planet's history, nothing on it was bigger than a microbe.
Four and a half billion years. The age of the Earth. And thirteen point eight billion years. The age of the universe.

This is the top of the past. Every event that has ever happened, fits below this line. The first stars lit up only a couple of hundred million years after the Big Bang. We arrived very late to this story.
Now the ladder keeps going, into the future. In about a billion years, the Sun will have brightened enough to boil away the oceans. In about five billion, it swells into a red giant.
Our galaxy and Andromeda are falling toward each other. A twenty twenty five study put the chance of a collision at roughly fifty fifty, within ten billion years.
Somewhere between a trillion and a hundred trillion years from now, the gas runs out. New stars stop forming. The last red dwarfs, flicker, and go dark.
Every star you have ever seen, will be a memory. If anyone is there to remember.
Ten to the thirty four years. Physicists have watched tanks of ultra pure water, deep underground, waiting for a single proton to decay. None ever has.
So we know a proton lives longer than ten to the thirty four years. If it dies at all.
Ten to the sixty seven years. A black hole as heavy as the Sun, finally finishes evaporating, through Hawking radiation.
It is the slowest fire in all of physics. It burns for longer than the universe has existed, by a number with sixty digits.
Ten to the hundred years. The last supermassive black holes, if nothing else intervenes, are gone.

What remains is a thin, cold haze of particles and light. The leading forecast is not a collapse. It is a fading. Nothing happens, ever again. That is the heat death of the universe. And it is a forecast, not a certainty.
Now look back at the ladder. All hundred and fifty rungs. And find where you are.

If the universe lasts as long as the forecast says, then we are living in the first tiny sliver of its entire story. The stars are still burning. The galaxies are still bright. We are astonishingly early.
The universe has barely begun. And you are one of the first minds it has ever had, to look back at itself.
Here is the practical part. You do not live on a hundred and fifty rungs. You live on about ten.

Seconds, where your attention is spent. Days, where habits are built. Years, where lives change. A few rare people live on the rungs above, building things that outlast them. Bridges. Books. Cathedrals. Ideas.
Decide which rung you are building for. Then act on the rung below it, today.
So here is the ladder, one last time. The shortest instant. The longest silence. And one second, somewhere in the middle, that you are spending right now.
Spend it like you know the numbers.
I hid seven golden hourglasses in this film. How many did you find? Write the number below. And tell me which rung stunned you most. Next time, the same journey, through space instead of time.
Thank you for watching.
